HuYgTa-e82927-d1e114.summary: Title paragraph restating the question in verse-like rubric form: whether any spiritual substance whatever exists in a place.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e123.summary: States the formal question to be disputed: whether every spiritual substance is in a place.
claims: The question to be resolved is whether every spiritual substance is in a place.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e128.summary: Opening argument for the affirmative: since God, the most spiritual and immaterial of all spirits, is in a place, no other substance can be excluded from place on the grounds of its spirituality. The premise that God is in a place is supported by an appeal to Augustine (any thing in which God is absent would revert to nothing, as things made from nothing), and by the claim that place is a real thing outside the mind (a species of the real predicament of quantity), so that since many real, non-annihilated places exist, God must truly be in place.
claims: If it is fitting for God, the most spiritual substance, to be in a place, then no other spiritual substance can be excluded from place by reason of its spirituality.
Place is a real extramental thing, a species of the predicament of quantity, so if real places exist that have not reverted to nothing, God (who sustains them) must be truly in place.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e165.summary: Argument for the negative, appealing to Boethius: the common conception of the mind is that incorporeal, i.e. spiritual, things are not in place. The paragraph then sets up the four-fold division of spiritual substance (uncreated, i.e. God; and created, which is threefold: intellectual as angel, rational as the human intellective soul, and universal as the abstracted nature of a corporeal thing considered according to cognized being) and announces that the question's four articles will correspond to these four kinds: whether God, whether an angel, whether the rational soul, and whether universal nature is in a place.
claims: The common conception (per Boethius) holds that spiritual/incorporeal things are not in place.
Spiritual substance divides fourfold: uncreated (God) and created, which is intellectual (angel), rational (human soul), or universal (abstracted nature).

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e199.summary: States the author's resolutio (summary answer) in advance of the articles: God is neither circumscriptively nor definitively determined by place, although he alone is perceived everywhere by his contact and conservation of things; an angel, however, is defined by place through its operation, and though it cannot be in several places simultaneously, it can be moved from place to place without contradiction.
claims: God is present to all places attingently and conservatively, but is neither circumscriptively nor definitively located.
An angel is defined in place through its operation, cannot be simultaneously in several places, but can move from place to place.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e217.summary: Heading paragraph for Article 1, restating its question: whether God is in a place.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e228.summary: States three conclusions to be proved for Article 1: (1) God is not in any place locally, neither circumscriptively nor determinatively; (2) God is in every place attingently and conservatively; (3) being simply everywhere belongs to God alone.
claims: God is not in place either circumscriptively or determinatively.
God is in every place by contact and conservation.
Being simply everywhere (ubique) belongs to God alone.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e244.summary: Proves the first conclusion: whatever is simply infinite cannot be circumscriptively or determinatively in a place, since anything circumscribed by place is somehow commensurate with it, and anything determined to a determinate place is there and not elsewhere, hence finite; but God is simply infinite, so God cannot be so located.
claims: What is simply infinite cannot be circumscriptively or determinatively in place, because such location entails commensuration with, or restriction to, a place, which entails finitude; God is simply infinite, therefore God is not so located.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e266.summary: States the second conclusion: God is everywhere, i.e., in every place, attingently and conservatively.
claims: God is in every place by way of contact and conservation, not by local circumscription.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e276.summary: Proves the second conclusion by analogy: just as an infinite magnitude of bulk, if it existed, would occupy every place (per Physics I), so an infinite magnitude of virtue/power reaches every place by contact and conservation; supports this with a scriptural citation (Wisdom 8) that divine Wisdom 'reaches from end to end mightily and disposes all things sweetly.'
claims: As an infinite bodily magnitude would occupy every place, so infinite power reaches and conserves every place.
concepts: magnitude of power vs. magnitude of bulk

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e306.summary: Second proof (argument 2) for God's universal presence: a spiritual substance is where it operates; God operates in all things (per the author of the Liber de causis, the primary cause influences more than the secondary cause), therefore God, as first cause of every particular cause, contributes more to the being of any effect than does its immediate secondary cause, and so is present wherever it operates, i.e., everywhere.
claims: A spiritual substance is present where it operates.
God, as first cause, operates in and contributes more to every effect than any secondary cause, and so is present in all things.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e327.summary: Third proof: whatever contains all things attingently/conservatively so that they do not slip into non-being is in all things this way; God is such, per Augustine's Confessions (addressing God: you do not need to be contained, since you contain all things; you fill by containing, not as vessels that would spill if broken; when you pour yourself out over us, you do not lie prostrate but raise us up); Anselm's Monologion is invoked to conclude that since nothing can exist or be conserved without God, God must be said to be everywhere and always.
claims: God contains and conserves all things so they do not fall into non-being, and is therefore present in all things attingently and conservatively.
Since nothing can exist or be conserved without God, God must be everywhere and always.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e364.summary: Raises an objection: it belongs to the nature of place that nothing located can be outside its place (per Physics II: it is fitting for a place to contain what it is the place of, neither greater nor less than what is located); hence it seems God must be in one place only, or nowhere, and so cannot be everywhere.
claims: If place by nature must exactly contain what is located, then God could only be in one place or in none, contradicting his omnipresence.
concepts: containment relation between place and located thing

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e385.summary: Responds briefly that the Philosopher there speaks of what is locally and circumscriptively in a place; the objection's premise about place must likewise be understood of that kind of place, which does not apply to God's mode of presence.
claims: Aristotle's definition of place in Physics II applies only to circumscriptive location, not to God's attingent/conservative presence.
concepts: distinguishing modes of 'being in a place'

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e398.summary: States the third conclusion with its proof: being everywhere per se and simply is proper to God alone, since a property is what belongs to something alone, always, and is convertibly predicated of it; per se and simply being everywhere fits God in just this way (per Porphyry's account of property), as follows from what precedes.
claims: Being everywhere per se and simply is a proprium of God alone, since it belongs to him alone, always, and convertibly.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e420.summary: First objection against the third conclusion: if there were only one human being, the human soul would be everywhere (since it is whole in the whole body it enlivens and whole in each part), so being everywhere would not belong to God alone by virtue of belonging to him alone.
claims: A hypothetical counterexample: if only one human existed, the soul (whole in the whole body and whole in each part) would seem to be everywhere, threatening the claim that ubiquity is proper to God alone.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e438.summary: Second objection: per the Philosopher, universals are everywhere and always, so ubiquity would not belong to God alone.
claims: If universals are everywhere and always (per Aristotle), then God is not the sole possessor of ubiquity.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e447.summary: Third objection: wherever there is body, there is necessarily matter; but there is body in every place, since a vacuum is impossible (per Physics IV); therefore matter is everywhere, and not God alone.
claims: Since a vacuum is impossible and body exists in every place, matter would be everywhere too, contradicting that ubiquity belongs to God alone.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e466.summary: Fourth objection: whatever does not belong to God from eternity does not belong to him always; but being everywhere did not belong to God from eternity, since every 'where' (ubi) was made in time; therefore being everywhere is not always proper to God (threatening the 'always' clause of the proprium definition).
claims: Since every spatial 'where' began in time, God's ubiquity could not have obtained from eternity, seemingly conflicting with the requirement that a proprium hold always.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e477.summary: Responds to the first objection: from the hypothetical case it does not follow that the soul would be everywhere per se and simply, but only per accidens, given that particular posited case.
claims: The soul's hypothetical omnipresence in the single-human scenario would be merely accidental, not per se and simple, so it does not undermine God's exclusive proprium.
concepts: per se vs. per accidens presence

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e488.summary: Responds to the second objection: universals are said to be everywhere not positively but privatively, since properly speaking they are nowhere per se; insofar as they are universal they abstract from individuating conditions (the here and now), and consequently abstract from 'where' and place altogether.
claims: Universals are 'everywhere' only privatively (by abstraction from place), not positively as God is.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e505.summary: Responds to the third objection: matter is in every place only per accidens, insofar as body of the predicament of substance happens to be there — which the author qualifies because in the place occupied by the accidents of the Eucharist there is no substantial body, only body of the predicament of quantity, and there is no strictly identical matter in different places but rather different portions of matter, unlike God who is the identical God in every place.
claims: Matter's presence in every place is only per accidens, tied to wherever substantial body happens to be, and involves numerically different portions of matter in different places — unlike God, who is identically present everywhere.
concepts: numerical identity of divine presence vs. matter

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e529.summary: Responds to the fourth objection: for God to be everywhere is for God to be in all things such that no thing exists in which God is not; hence God was everywhere from eternity even while existing only in himself, since no other thing existed. In other things God began to be in time, not through a change in himself but through a change in those things; correspondingly things were in God from eternity — not by the stability of the things themselves but by the stability and entity of God, since whatever is in something is in it according to the mode of that in which it is; so things are in God eternally while God is in things temporally, since things are measured by time but God by eternity.
claims: God's being everywhere is his being in all things such that none lacks him; his 'beginning' to be in creatures in time reflects a change in the creatures, not in God.
Things exist in God eternally (by God's mode of being) even though God exists in things temporally (by their mode of being), since things are measured by time and God by eternity.
concepts: divine immutability amid apparent temporal presence

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e558.summary: Heading paragraph for Article 2, restating its question: whether an angel is in a place.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e571.summary: States three conclusions to be proved for Article 2: (1) an angel is in a place; (2) one angel cannot be in several places at once; (3) an angel is moved from place to place.
claims: An angel is in a place.
An angel cannot be simultaneously in several places.
An angel can move from place to place.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e584.summary: First proof of the first conclusion (argument 1): a thing is in place through its quantity; but an angel's power/virtue, taken not absolutely but in comparison to an object and operation, is its 'quantity'; therefore an angel can truly be said to be in some place or body insofar as it truly and really applies its power in operating around that place. Explains that virtue is not called quantity in relation to substance (where it would be a quality, a good disposition of its possessor perfecting it) but rather in the order to its object, per Avicenna's Sufficientia.
claims: A thing is located through its quantity; an angel's 'quantity' consists in its power considered relationally, in order to its object and operation — hence an angel is in place through the real application of its power via operation.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e619.summary: Second proof (argument 2), from Damascene: an angel is where it operates.
claims: Per Damascene, an angel is present where it operates.
concepts: operation as criterion of angelic location

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e629.summary: Third proof (argument 3): whatever has finite and limited power is necessarily defined by place, and thus is definitively in a place; an angel's power is finite and limited; therefore an angel is defined by place. Just as God is everywhere because his power's quantity is infinite, so a being with finite, determinate power will be in a determinate place.
claims: Finite, limited power entails definitive location in place; an angel's power is finite, so an angel is definitively located, in contrast to God's infinite power grounding ubiquity.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e651.summary: Introduces a series of counterarguments (some direct, some indirect) against the view that an angel's operation is the reason it is in a place. First direct counterargument: if an angel's operation were the reason for its being in place, that operation would have to be either immanent or transient; not immanent, since understanding and willing are no less abstracted from spatial position than the angel's essence itself (so if the essence is not the reason for being in place, neither is this operation); not transient either, since just as quantity existing in one body cannot be another body's reason for being circumscriptively in place, a transient operation existing in the thing moved cannot be another's reason for being determinatively in place.
claims: If operation grounded an angel's location, it would have to be either immanent operation (ruled out because such operation is as abstracted from place as the angel's essence) or transient operation (ruled out by an analogy with quantity, which cannot locate a different body).

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e682.summary: Second counterargument: if transient operation were the reason for definitive location, then a body moving another body would simultaneously be in two places — circumscriptively in one through its own quantity, and definitively in another through its operation.
claims: If transient operation grounded definitive location, a moving body would absurdly be in two places at once, one circumscriptively and one definitively.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e698.summary: Third counterargument: as operating relates to being, so operating in place relates to being in place; but operation always presupposes being; therefore operating in place always presupposes being in place, so operation cannot be the reason for being in place, since a cause does not presuppose its effect but the reverse.
claims: Since operation presupposes being (and analogously, operating-in-place presupposes being-in-place), operation cannot be the cause of being in place without inverting the cause-effect relation.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e716.summary: Fourth counterargument: if operation were the reason for being in place, then since the heaven (caelum) operates on an egg or a grain of millet, the heaven would be in the egg or grain of millet.
claims: The 'operation grounds location' thesis leads to the absurdity that the heavens would be located inside an egg or grain of millet on which they act.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e727.summary: Fifth counterargument: since an angel existing in the Empyrean heaven does not operate around any body there, it would follow that the angel existing in the Empyrean would not be in a place.
claims: If location depends on operation around a body, an angel in the Empyrean heaven (which is not acted upon) would seem to be in no place at all.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e739.summary: Sixth counterargument: an angel passing from heaven to earth could traverse the middle region operating on nothing in it; it would then be in no place at all during transit, since while moving it is neither in the terminus from which nor the terminus to which, nor in the middle (since, as supposed, it operates on nothing there).
claims: An angel in local transit that acts on nothing in the intervening medium would, on the operation-based account, be located nowhere during its motion — an absurd consequence.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e759.summary: Seventh counterargument (an 'indirect' one): if operating around some corporeal thing were the precise reason for being in place, then God — who can and does operate around corporeal things — would be in place, which is unacceptable.
claims: Operation-based location would imply, absurdly, that God is in place, since God too operates on corporeal things.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e779.summary: Eighth counterargument: whatever belongs to something in every respect apart from its substance belongs to it precisely through its substance; but being in a place belongs to an angel apart from its substance in every other circumscribed respect; therefore being in place belongs to the angel through its substance (not through operation).
claims: By a general inferential pattern, since being-in-place is not distinguished among the angel's other non-substantial features, it must belong to the angel through its substance rather than through operation.
concepts: inference from constancy across non-substantial features to substantial ground

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e790.summary: Ninth counterargument, invoking the Parisian Article (the 1277 condemnations): it is condemned as an error to hold that an angel is in a place through its operation alone, such that being in a place would in no way belong to it through its substance.
claims: The Parisian Article condemns as erroneous the claim that an angel is in place solely through operation and not at all through substance.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e799.summary: Tenth counterargument: if an angel's operation were the reason for its being in a place, this would be because that on which it operates is in a place; but an angel often operates on things that are not in a place, e.g., when it applies its power to the outermost heaven or to some separate substance; hence in those cases it would not be in any place.
claims: Since angels sometimes operate on things not themselves in a place (the outermost heaven, separate substances), an operation-based account would wrongly imply the angel is then in no place.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e815.summary: Rejects the foregoing counterarguments as inconclusive and begins the replies. Reply to the first: the operation by which an angel is in place need not be a transmutation of body but is the application of its power; granting that this application is 'in' the applying angel and hence of equal abstraction from matter as the angel's essence, it is nevertheless not of equal abstraction from quantity in the mode by which quantity is taken in things separated from matter, since virtual quantity is known in relation to an object through operation.
claims: An angel's locating operation is not a bodily transmutation but the application of its power; this application, while as immaterial as the angel's essence, is not equally abstracted from (virtual) quantity, which is grasped relationally through operation on an object.
concepts: abstraction from matter vs. abstraction from quantity

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e840.summary: Reply to the second counterargument: a body moving another body is in the same place both circumscriptively and definitively, so no absurdity of double location in two different places arises.
claims: The mover-body objection is resolved by noting the mover is circumscriptively and definitively in the same place, not two different places.
concepts: coincidence of circumscriptive and definitive presence in the same place

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e849.summary: Reply to the third counterargument: although absolutely speaking operating presupposes being, not every determinate operating presupposes a correspondingly determinate being in that respect, since sometimes such being arises from the operating itself — just as not every act of playing the cithara presupposes already being a cithara-player, since one becomes a cithara-player by playing. Similarly, though an angel's operating presupposes the angel's being, the angel's operating in a place does not presuppose the angel's already being in that place, since that mode of being arises from the operating.
claims: Operating in a place need not presuppose already being in that place, by analogy with acquiring a skill (cithara-playing) through the very act that constitutes it.
concepts: operari not always presupposing determinate esse

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e875.summary: Reply to the fourth counterargument: a thing can operate either mediately or immediately on something; if immediately, then by that operation it is determined and defined to that place; not so if it operates mediately. Since the heaven operates only mediately on the lower bodies (the egg, the grain of millet), the argument does not conclude that the heaven is located in them.
claims: Mediate operation does not locate the operating agent where the mediate effect occurs; only immediate operation does — resolving the heaven/egg absurdity.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e893.summary: Reply to the fifth counterargument: although an angel may lack operation moving the Empyrean heaven itself, it can still apply its power to that heaven through its own intellection and volition.
claims: An angel present in the Empyrean is still located there via the application of its power through intellection and volition, even absent a moving operation on the heaven.
concepts: intellection and volition as modes of applying virtue

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e906.summary: Reply to the sixth counterargument: at no time or instant can an angel be so idle that it applies its power to no corporeal being at all.
claims: An angel is never wholly inactive with respect to some corporeal being, so the transit-through-an-inert-medium scenario does not arise as posited.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e917.summary: Notes that other authors add a further qualification: granted that an angel were sometimes idle in this way, then for that span it would not be actually but only aptitudinally in a place.
claims: Even conceding a hypothetical idle angel, it would be in a place only 'aptitudinally' (potentially), not actually, for that span.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e929.summary: Reply to the seventh counterargument: the inference would hold if God were of finite power; but because of the infinity of his power, God is not defined or determined to one place, but is everywhere and in every place — so the argument that would locate God does not apply to him.
claims: The God-in-place absurdity does not follow, since God's infinite power (unlike an angel's finite power) grounds omnipresence rather than definitive location.
concepts: disanalogy between finite angelic power and infinite divine power

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e942.summary: Reply to the eighth counterargument: the minor premise is simply false, so the argument does not conclude.
claims: The eighth counterargument's minor premise is denied outright.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e951.summary: Gives an alternative reply found elsewhere: the minor is false because an angel's (virtual) quantity is not attended to immediately according to the angel's substance, so the argument does not conclude.
claims: An alternative rebuttal: angelic virtual quantity is not immediately grounded in substance, so the objection's minor premise fails.
concepts: virtual quantity not immediate to substance

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e962.summary: Reply to the ninth counterargument (the Parisian Article): our doctor (Aegidius Romanus, the 'doctor noster') does not deny that angels are in a place; he only denies that the angel's essence is the immediate reason for its being in place — so the Article is in no way against the doctor's position.
claims: The Parisian condemnation is not actually opposed to the author's (Giles of Rome's) view, since he affirms angels are in place but denies essence is the immediate ground of that location.
concepts: reconciling the Parisian Article with the doctor's position

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e975.summary: Reply to the tenth counterargument: denies the minor premise outright, and to its proof responds that even the outermost heaven is at least per accidens in a place; moreover an angel never applies its power to a separate substance in such a way that this application ceases with respect to every body, since at the very least it wills to be in whatever place it is then in, and such willing is itself a kind of operation, i.e., an application of its power.
claims: The outermost heaven is at least accidentally in place; an angel's application of power to a separate substance never fully detaches it from bodily location, since its will to be somewhere is itself a locating operation.
concepts: outermost heaven per accidens in place

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e997.summary: Introduces further, 'indirect' counterarguments against the first conclusion, reporting a rival position: some say an angel is nowhere in the sense of owing a definitive place or situs, but is present everywhere to every body by presence of order, not presence of situs, whether or not it moves a body; presence of an angel to a place is said to precede its operation there, since every action presupposes the presence of agent and patient — operation does not make the agent's essence present to the patient but presupposes it.
claims: A reported rival view: angelic presence is a non-local 'presence of order' to all bodies, logically prior to and independent of operation, since action presupposes rather than causes the agent's presence to the patient.
concepts: presence of order vs. presence of situs

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1027.summary: Rejects the reported rival view, giving a first counter (argument 1): it would make the angel everywhere, which belongs to God alone, as shown in the third conclusion of Article 1.
claims: The 'presence of order' view wrongly grants angels the ubiquity that belongs to God alone.
concepts: cross-reference to Article 1's third conclusion on divine ubiquity

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1039.summary: Second counter (argument 2): whatever's essence extends to being everywhere present, its power extends to operating everywhere; so if an angel's essence were simultaneously present to every body, as the rival view claims, its power could simultaneously operate on every body, which is impossible.
claims: If essence-presence entailed power to operate wherever present, the rival view's universal angelic presence would absurdly grant angels power to operate everywhere at once.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1052.summary: Third counter (argument 3): if God made another world, would the angel deemed present to every body of this world also be present to every body of that second world? If yes, then were God to make infinite worlds, the angel would be present to every body of every world — impossible, since then each angel would be infinite; if no, then the angel is definitively in this world, and hence in this body now, and not present to every body.
claims: A dilemma against universal angelic presence: extending it across possible additional worlds either makes the angel infinite (absurd) or forces the concession that the angel is in fact definitively located in this world.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1074.summary: Fourth counter (argument 4): the rival opinion expressly contradicts Damascene, who says that angels, when in heaven, are not on earth, and when sent to earth by God do not remain in heaven.
claims: Damascene's testimony (angels are not simultaneously in heaven and on earth) directly contradicts the rival 'universal presence' opinion.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1086.summary: Reports a second rival position: others say that an angel is in a place through its very essence, such that the essence itself is the reason the angel is in a determinate place.
claims: A second reported rival view: the angel's essence itself (not merely its power/operation) is the direct ground of its being in a determinate place.
concepts: essence as immediate ground of location (rejected view)

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1097.summary: First argument for this second rival view: as an infinite being relates to being everywhere, so a finite being relates to being somewhere; God, because of the infinity of his essence, is everywhere; therefore an angel, because of the limitation of its essence, is in a determinate place.
claims: By analogy with divine infinity grounding ubiquity, an angel's finite essence would ground its being in a determinate place.
concepts: analogy of infinite/finite essence to ubiquity/determinate location

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1109.summary: Second argument: by nature the active is present to the passive prior to acting upon it.
claims: Presence of agent to patient is naturally prior to the agent's acting, supporting essence (not operation) as the ground of presence.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1116.summary: Third argument: an angel according to its essence cannot be outside the universe, since a part is not outside its whole, nor can it be everywhere in the universe (since then the part would equal its whole); therefore it will be somewhere in the universe, and consequently definitively in a place according to its own essence.
claims: An angel as a 'part' of the universe cannot be outside it nor coextensive with it, and so must be definitively somewhere in it, by its very essence.
concepts: part-whole relation of angel to universe

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1129.summary: Fourth argument, citing the Parisian Article: it condemns as an error the claim that a separated soul or an angel is nowhere according to substance.
claims: The Parisian Article condemns the claim that a separated soul or angel is nowhere according to substance, supporting the essence-based view of location.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1140.summary: Rejects this second rival view too: a thing is in place according as it is fitting for it to be quantified (per Avicenna's Sufficientia), but being quantified does not belong to an angel according to its essence, as is evident of itself.
claims: The essence-based view fails because location tracks quantity, and quantity does not belong to angelic essence as such.
concepts: quantity as the ground of location, not essence

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1157.summary: Cites a certain 'solemn doctor' on Book 2 (identified conventionally as Henry of Ghent) in support: all the masters agree that essence is not the reason a thing is in place.
claims: An authoritative doctor's Quodlibet is cited as attesting to a broad scholarly consensus that essence is not the ground of being in place.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1171.summary: Reply to the first argument of the second rival view: the infinity of essence is not, on our way of understanding, the immediate reason God is everywhere; rather it is the quantity or magnitude of his power, by which God is in all things — since in all things he operates all that is produced (by producing) and all that persists in being (by conserving).
claims: It is God's operative power, not his essence's infinity per se, that is the immediate ground of divine ubiquity, contra the rival analogy.
concepts: power (not essence) as immediate ground of ubiquity

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1190.summary: Reply to the second argument: although operation presupposes the presence of agent and patient, this need not by definition presuppose local presence — presence extends more broadly than local presence. One can also say that granting the action presupposes the agent's presence, that presence itself presupposes the quantity of the agent's power, by which quantity a separated agent (of the kind here under discussion) is in place.
claims: Presence in general is broader than local presence; even if operation presupposes presence, that presence in turn presupposes the virtual quantity that is itself the ground of an angel's location.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1214.summary: Reply to the third argument: we concede an angel is somewhere, but not immediately through its essence — rather through its power and operation.
claims: Angels are located somewhere, but the immediate ground is power/operation, not essence, contra the part-whole argument.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1225.summary: Reply to the fourth argument (the Parisian Article): the Article is explained by another authority as meaning that an angel is 'nowhere according to substance' in the sense that substance is not the reason for being in place, not in the sense that substance itself is not in place — so understood, it is true that the angel is 'nowhere according to substance,' and the Article turns out to support rather than oppose the author's position.
claims: Properly interpreted, the Parisian Article condemns denying that the angel's substance is in place at all, not denying that substance is the reason for location — so it actually favors the author's view.
concepts: distinguishing 'is in place' from 'is the reason for being in place'

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1251.summary: States the second conclusion of Article 2 with its own proof: considering an angel's natural power, it cannot be simultaneously in several distinct places, since just as a creature is by nature determined to one species, so by its quantity (virtual) it is determined, at least for the same time, to one place. Notes that the Master (Lombard) seems to hold this conclusion, since he proves in the text, by several authorities, that an angel is defined by place, or determined to a place.
claims: An angel's natural power determines it to one place at a time, just as its nature determines it to one species; this matches Lombard's own textual position.
concepts: determination to species vs. determination to place

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1271.summary: First objection against the second conclusion: what is a mean partakes of the nature of the extremes; an angel is a kind of mean between corporeal nature and God; therefore, since corporeal nature is only in one place and God is in every place (since he is everywhere), the angel would be simultaneously in several places.
claims: A 'mean between extremes' argument suggests the angel, mediating between wholly localized bodies and the omnipresent God, should be in multiple places at once.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1287.summary: Second objection: one body can be in different places simultaneously (by divine power, per later discussion), therefore so can one spirit; the antecedent is proved because it is no more repugnant to a body to have two extrinsic relations (respectus) at once than two intrinsic ones, and a body can have two intrinsic relations at once (e.g., the same whiteness grounds simultaneous likeness to many white things), so it should be able to have several situs at once, since situs denotes an extrinsic relation.
claims: An argument from the possibility of multi-location for bodies (via divine power) and from the compatibility of multiple relations in one subject, extended to angelic multi-location.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1312.summary: Third objection (proving the antecedent 'at least as a possibility'): as several bodies relate to one place, so one body relates to several places; but by divine power two bodies can be in one place at once, as when a glorified body passes through another body; therefore (by parity) one body could be in several places, supporting angelic multi-location by analogy.
claims: Analogical proportion argument: since divine power allows two bodies in one place (as with a glorified body passing through another), it should likewise allow one body in several places, and by extension an angel in several places.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1325.summary: Fourth objection: whatever God can do by means of a secondary cause, he can do without it; but by means of the conversion of bread in the Eucharist, the body of Christ is by divine power on multiple altars; therefore even without such conversion the same power could make the same body be in different places — especially since the secondary cause here is not intrinsic, and the minor is evident from faith.
claims: An argument from Eucharistic multi-presence of Christ's body (via transubstantiation) to the more general possibility of one body being in different places even without such conversion.
concepts: principle that what God does via a secondary cause he can do without it

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1343.summary: Dismisses the last two proofs (the Eucharistic and glorified-body arguments) as beside the point, since the present conclusion concerns natural power, not God's absolute power; defers full treatment of whether a body or angel can by absolute power be simultaneously in several places, and how, to Book 4, distinction 10.
claims: The Eucharistic/glorified-body proofs address absolute divine power, which is irrelevant to the present conclusion about an angel's natural power; the topic is deferred to Book 4, d.10.
concepts: natural power vs. absolute divine power

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1359.summary: Reply to the first objection (the 'mean' argument): an angel holds a mean not with respect to plurality of places but with respect to the mode of being in place, since God is neither circumscriptively nor definitively in place, while a body is both circumscriptively and definitively in place, and the angel as a mean is definitively but not circumscriptively in place.
claims: The angel's mediating status concerns the mode of location (definitive without circumscription), not multiplicity of places, resolving the 'mean' objection.
concepts: angel as mean in mode of presence, not in number of places

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1377.summary: Reply to the second objection: denies the antecedent, and to its proof says the comparison is not apt, since likeness denotes a pure relation with the same foundation remaining, so multiplying only the terms multiplies the likenesses; situs, however, does not denote a pure relation, since all six 'principles' (the accidental categories including situs) denote an absolute thing, though connoting or falling under a relation.
claims: Situs is not a purely relational accident like likeness, so the analogy allowing multiple likenesses from one foundation does not transfer to allowing multiple situs from one subject.
concepts: pure relation vs. relation-connoting absolute (the sex principia)

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1397.summary: Reply to the second and third objections' remaining proofs: concedes them, since they argue from divine (absolute) power rather than from the nature of the thing.
claims: The proofs invoking divine power are conceded as true of absolute power but irrelevant to the natural-power conclusion under discussion.
concepts: distinguishing arguments from nature vs. from divine power

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1407.summary: Notes that a proponent of the opposite opinion would reply differently to the second proof: the cases are not alike, because divine power can, without contradiction, remove from a body's dimensions their extrinsic effect of resisting other dimensions (by which one body does not tolerate another in the same situs), whereas one and the same body being circumscriptively here and elsewhere in the same mode would imply a contradiction (it would be here and not be here), since what is circumscribed in one place cannot be circumscribed elsewhere.
claims: An alternative response (from a rival school) distinguishes removing bodily impenetrability (non-contradictory) from one body being circumscriptively in two places under the same mode (contradictory).
concepts: impenetrability as an extrinsic effect of dimension

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1433.summary: Continues this alternative reply to the third proof (the Eucharistic argument): God makes Christ's body be in several places at once neither by conversion nor without conversion in a circumscriptive manner according to the same dimensions, so the argument does not conclude a genuine circumscriptive multilocation.
claims: The Eucharistic presence of Christ's body in multiple places is not circumscriptive multilocation according to the same dimensions, blocking the inference to bodily circumscriptive multilocation generally.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1451.summary: States the third conclusion of Article 2 with proofs: an angel is moved locally. First proof: whatever changes place is moved locally; an angel changes place, per Damascene, Book 2. Second proof: the separated soul is moved locally (an article of faith holds that Christ's soul descended to the underworld), therefore so is the angel, since as a complete supposit the angel has no less claim to being able to move than the soul, which lacks the character of a complete supposit while separated from the body.
claims: An angel is moved locally, proved both by Damascene's testimony and by analogy with the separated soul's local motion (attested by Christ's descent to the underworld).
concepts: descent of Christ's soul (article of faith)

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1477.summary: Raises a possible objection: if an angel is moved, then it has matter as part of itself, since Metaphysics II says one must imagine matter in everything that is moved.
claims: An objection from Aristotle's Metaphysics II: motion seems to require matter, threatening the claim that an immaterial angel can be moved.
concepts: matter as presupposed by motion (Metaphysics II)

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1489.summary: A further point (labeled '3'): if an angel is moved, it will have part and part, since Physics VIII proves that whatever is moved is partly in the terminus from which and partly in the terminus to which.
claims: A second worry from Physics VIII: motion implies partial location in successive termini, which seems to require the mobile to have parts, again threatening angelic (partless) motion.
concepts: successive partial location in motion (Physics VIII)

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1501.summary: Responds that these two Aristotelian texts must be understood of what is moved in such a way that it is commensurate with the space over which it moves, not of other kinds of motion (such as an angel's).
claims: Aristotle's texts on matter and partial location in motion apply only to spatially commensurate motion, not to angelic motion, resolving both objections.
concepts: restricting Aristotelian motion-texts to spatially commensurate motion

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1513.summary: Raises the difficult further question whether an angel moves in time or in an instant. Following the author's own doctor (Aegidius Romanus), concludes the angel's motion occurs in time, because wherever there is succession, it is somehow measured by time; and there is succession in both the angel's immanent acts (understanding and willing — an angel does not understand everything at once, nor is its intellect informed by several species at once, so even without discursive reasoning there is succession in its acts of understanding, and Augustine, De Genesi ad litteram VIII, accordingly says the angel is moved 'through times') and its transient acts (it does not operate on all bodies simultaneously; and, per the doctrine already established, being-in-place follows from operating on a body, so succession of such operations is called local motion).
claims: Following Aegidius Romanus, the angel's motion (both the succession internal to its acts of understanding/willing and the succession of its transient operations on bodies) occurs in time, not in a bare instant.
Augustine (De Genesi ad litteram VIII) supports describing angelic change as occurring 'through times.'

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1565.summary: Notes, apropos of certain sayings of Augustine, that all succession is reducible to a temporal measure; and since the immediate succession in angelic motion is a succession of operations, with local variation/succession being attended to only by means of the succession of those operations, such motion is more properly called motion 'through times' than 'through places.' This is perhaps why Augustine (De Genesi ad litteram VIII) simply denies that a spiritual creature moves through places, asserting instead that it changes through times.
claims: Local variation in angelic motion is mediated by, and secondary to, the succession of operations, which is why the motion is more properly temporal than local — explaining Augustine's denial of angelic local motion in favor of temporal change.
concepts: priority of temporal succession over local succession in angelic motion
Augustine's denial of spiritual local motion

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1592.summary: Introduces the contrary position, which holds that an angel moves in an instant. First argument for it: spiritual substance is of greater power than corporeal things; but the sun multiplies its rays from east to west in an instant (per De Anima II); therefore (a fortiori) an angel moves instantaneously.
claims: A reported opposing view (instantaneous angelic motion) argues from the sun's instantaneous ray-propagation to the greater power of spiritual substance.
concepts: instantaneous propagation of light (De Anima II)
argument a fortiori from lesser to greater power

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1611.summary: Second argument for instantaneous motion: if an angel moved in time, then a body and an angel would move equally fast, which is false since spiritual substance is always more vigorous than corporeal; the consequence is proved because God could make a body whose heaviness or lightness so exceeds that of the body which moves in time with the angel, by an amount proportional to how much the time measuring the body's motion exceeds the time measuring the angel's, that this newly-made body would move in the same time and at the same speed as the angel.
claims: A quantitative argument: if angelic motion took time, God could construct a body matching the angel's speed exactly, absurdly equating angelic and corporeal velocity — hence angelic motion must be instantaneous.
concepts: comparability of motion-times as an argument against temporal angelic motion

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1635.summary: Third argument: the intellective soul moves in an instant, therefore so does the angel; the antecedent is proved because in the duration during which a person is corrupted and dies, the soul does not remain in the body (otherwise it would simultaneously die and live), but the corruption of a human being occurs in an instant, so the soul departs the body in an instant.
claims: An argument from the instantaneous character of a human's death (soul's departure) to the instantaneous character of angelic/soul motion generally.
concepts: instant of death as departure of the soul

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1651.summary: Begins counterarguments against the instantaneous-motion opinion. First: what acts in an instant does not act first in one part rather than another; but an angel cannot act this way without acting first in one part rather than another; therefore (its action, and by extension motion, is not instantaneous).
claims: Instantaneous causation should not privilege any part over another temporally, but angelic action does proceed part-by-part, telling against instantaneous angelic motion.
concepts: instantaneous action and absence of part-priority

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1670.summary: Second counterargument: every indivisible change (mutatio) is the terminus of some motion (per Physics VI), so an angel must first undergo a true, time-measured motion before being 'changed' (mutatum esse).
claims: Since indivisible change is the terminus of a properly durational motion (Physics VI), angelic 'change' presupposes a preceding time-measured motion, against pure instantaneity.
concepts: mutatio as terminus of motus (Physics VI)

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1683.summary: Third counterargument: as a point relates to a line, so an instant relates to time; by permutation, as a point relates to an instant, so a line relates to time; but a point cannot be traversed by any creature in less than an instant, therefore no creature can traverse a line in less than time — implying that if an angel moves per se, it must do so in time, not an instant, when traversing extended distances.
claims: A proportional (point:instant :: line:time) argument concludes that traversing any extended distance (a 'line') requires time, not a bare instant.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1701.summary: Fourth counterargument: an angel is not moved while in the terminus from which (motion not yet begun) nor while in the terminus to which (motion already ceased); therefore it must be moved in the middle; but if it were in the middle and in the terminus to which in the same instant, the angel would simultaneously be moved and at rest, a contradiction.
claims: A dilemma about the termini and middle of motion shows that collapsing motion into a single instant yields the contradiction of being simultaneously moved and at rest.
concepts: terminus a quo / terminus ad quem
contradiction of simultaneous motion and rest

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1721.summary: Fifth counterargument: the separated soul does not move in an instant, therefore neither does the angel, since the angel is of no greater velocity than the separated soul; the antecedent is proved because if the separated soul moved in an instant, it would (absurdly) be of lesser power in a glorified body than without it, since in such a body it cannot move in an instant.
claims: An argument from the non-instantaneous motion of the separated soul (proved via a comparison with the soul's motion in a glorified body) to the non-instantaneous motion of the angel.
concepts: comparison of separated soul with and without glorified body

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1739.summary: Sixth counterargument: if an angel moved in an instant, God could not move the angel more swiftly with his whole power than the angel moves itself, since no measure is shorter than an instant; but the consequent is false, since the same mobile is moved more swiftly by infinite power than by finite power.
claims: Instantaneous angelic motion would absurdly cap the effect of divine omnipotence at the angel's own natural speed, contradicting the principle that infinite power moves things faster than finite power.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1755.summary: Seventh counterargument: if an angel moved in an instant, it would simultaneously be in two places, since it would be simultaneously in the middle and in the terminus.
claims: Instantaneous motion would put the angel simultaneously in the medium and the terminus, i.e., in two places at once.
concepts: simultaneous double location as absurd consequence

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1767.summary: Concedes that although the conclusion (instantaneous motion is false / motion is temporal) is true, the seven preceding reasons, though of great apparent force, are not actually conclusive.
claims: The author judges the temporal-motion conclusion correct but finds the seven counterarguments just given individually inconclusive.
concepts: distinguishing a true conclusion from inconclusive arguments for it

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1776.summary: Reply to the first of the seven counterarguments: although a created agent by nature acts first on one part rather than another, it need not act first in duration on one part rather than another.
claims: Priority of action by nature does not entail priority in duration, resolving the 'part-priority' objection to instantaneous action.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1789.summary: Reply to the second: the Aristotelian proposition is not universally true among the faithful, since in the very first instant in which the sun was created it could illuminate, and yet no motion preceded that change of illumination.
claims: A theological counterexample (the sun's first-instant illumination at creation) shows the Aristotelian principle (change presupposes prior motion) is not universally binding for believers.
concepts: creation of the sun as counterexample to Aristotelian principle

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1800.summary: Reply to the third: the 'commutated proportion' (point:instant::line:time) does not hold unless made with respect to something intrinsic; since being of the genus of the permanent belongs to the nature of a point, as being of the genus of the fluent belongs to the nature of an instant, the proportion would validly conclude only if line were likewise permanent and time fluent in the same intrinsic sense — but traversal of a point or line is something extrinsic to them, so nothing follows; just as it does not follow that because a point cannot be marked twice in the same instant, a line cannot be marked twice in the same time, since such comparison concerns extrinsic features.
claims: The point:instant::line:time proportion fails because it conflates intrinsic natures (permanent point vs. fluent instant) with the extrinsic feature of traversal, blocking the inference used in the third counterargument.
concepts: intrinsic vs. extrinsic comparison in proportional arguments

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1833.summary: Reply to the fourth: at the first sign or instant in which the angel is in the terminus ad quem, it is not properly said to be 'at rest' but rather 'to have been changed' (mutatum esse); hence it does not follow that it simultaneously moves and rests, though it does follow that it simultaneously moves and has been changed — a feature common to all instantaneous changes, as when air is simultaneously being illuminated and has been illuminated.
claims: Distinguishing 'being at rest' from 'having been changed' dissolves the fourth counterargument's contradiction, by analogy with the simultaneous illumination and illuminatedness of air.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1853.summary: Reply to the fifth: the consequence can be denied, since the soul's power, naturally speaking, is less than an angel's; even granting the separated soul moves in an instant, the opponent could say it is not inconvenient that, once joined to a glorified body, it moves in time, since joined to a body it naturally follows the laws of that body — and this does not detract from the soul's perfection, since it is natural for it, as such, to move in time while conjoined to a body.
claims: A body-conjoined soul naturally follows bodily (temporal) laws of motion without loss of perfection, blocking the inference from separated-soul instantaneity to glorified-body instantaneity.
concepts: soul's motion conditioned by union with body
natural law of conjoined vs. separated states

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1883.summary: Reply to the sixth: an opponent would deny the consequence, holding that within the same instant there are several 'signs,' and that in a duration shorter than an instant God could move the angel, e.g., by one such sign; adds that by parity of reasoning one could argue God could not illuminate air faster than the sun does (since the sun illuminates in an instant), yet we must say God never acts with the full impetus of his power in a single act; hence a nature that does act with its whole impetus, though it may begin in a minimal duration and even attain the same velocity God would use for that effect, can still, in infinitely many other ways, fall short of divine power with respect to the same effect.
claims: A layered rebuttal to the sixth counterargument: instants can contain multiple 'signs' allowing finer gradations; and divine power's superiority over natural agents need not manifest as superior speed, since God does not exhaust his power in any single created effect.
concepts: plurality of signs within an instant
natural agent's maximal effort vs. infinite divine excess

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1916.summary: Reply to the seventh: an opponent would say that although it is impossible for a thing to be simultaneously in two places in a lasting/permanent way, it is not impossible for the same thing to be in two places transitively, i.e., unstably and transitorily.
claims: Distinguishing permanent from transitory/transitive double-location dissolves the seventh counterargument, since instantaneous motion would only produce the latter.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1929.summary: Transitional paragraph: to the arguments raised against the doctor (i.e., against Aegidius Romanus's temporal-motion view — the original arguments for instantaneous motion), the doctor himself responds by the following distinction.
concepts: transition to the doctor's own replies

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1936.summary: The doctor's reply to the first argument for instantaneous motion (the sun-ray argument): denies the comparison holds, since light is not itself moved through the air, but rather there are continuous generations of light in the air which, though instantaneous, are nonetheless simultaneously induced in the same instant even while one causally/originatively precedes another; since the angel's very same power is applied to the whole span at once, whereas one and the same species of light does not traverse the whole span, the analogy is nearly irrelevant to the present question.
claims: The sun-ray argument fails because light propagation is a series of simultaneous instantaneous generations, not a single moving entity traversing space the way an angel's applied power would have to — the cases are disanalogous.
concepts: light as successive instantaneous generation, not motion
disanalogy between light propagation and angelic power application

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1956.summary: Reply to the second argument (equal-speed absurdity): denies the consequence, since the time measuring an angel's motion is of a different kind (ratio) from the time measuring a body's motion, and so the two are not mutually comparable, nor can we arrive at their equality by abbreviating one relative to the other.
claims: Angelic and corporeal 'time' are incommensurable in kind, blocking the inference that temporal angelic motion would make it comparably fast to bodily motion.
concepts: incommensurability of angelic and corporeal time

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e1972.summary: Reply to the third argument (soul's instantaneous departure at death): the soul's separation, as a kind of corruption, is not properly a motion but a mutatio, and so can be measured in an instant. But if after death the soul remained in the body not as its form but as its mover (which the doctor considers quite possible), and were later separated as a mover is separated from its mobile, the same judgment would apply to the soul as to the angel, since then the soul would be truly moved apart from the body in such a way that one could mark a last instant of its being in that body and a first instant of its being outside it, and its motion, conceived temporally, would be measured within those two instants.
claims: Death as such is an instantaneous mutatio, not a motion — but if the soul persisted post-mortem as mover rather than form, its eventual separation would be a genuine (temporal) motion analogous to the angel's, bounded by a last and first instant.
concepts: mutatio vs. motus applied to death
soul as form vs. soul as mover

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e2004.summary: Heading paragraph for Article 3, restating its question: whether the rational soul is in a place.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e2013.summary: Very brief and textually corrupt paragraph stating that from what has already been said, it likewise appears what should be held concerning the third principal (article), i.e., that the treatment of the rational soul's presence in place follows analogously from the discussion of the angel in Article 2.
claims: The resolution of Article 3 (on the rational soul) is said to follow by analogy from the preceding treatment of the angel in Article 2, without a fresh extended proof.
concepts: analogical extension of Article 2's conclusions to the rational soul

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e2020.summary: Heading paragraph for Article 4, restating its question: whether universal nature is in a place.

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e2029.summary: Answers Article 4: just as universal nature is not generated per se but is generated only in the generation of another (i.e., of particulars, per the Liber sex principiorum), so too it is not moved per se; if any motion belongs to it at all, this belongs to it only in the mode of belonging to the motion of another, namely the motion of particulars.
claims: Universal nature, paralleling its mode of generation, is neither in place nor moved per se, but only derivatively through the particulars in which it is instantiated and which alone properly move.
concepts: universal nature generated only per accidens through particulars (Liber sex principiorum)

HuYgTa-e82927-d1e2049.summary: Closes Article 4 (and the question) by replying to the principal argument and to the contrary instance: no spiritual substance is circumscriptively in a place, and this is how Boethius's statement (that incorporeal things are not in place) should be understood — i.e., as denying circumscriptive location to spiritual substances, not denying definitive or attingent/conservative presence as established through the four articles.
claims: Boethius's dictum that spiritual things are not in place is to be understood as denying only circumscriptive location, consistent with the definitive location of angels/souls and the conservative omnipresence of God established across the four articles.
concepts: reconciling Boethius with the article's distinctions
circumscriptive vs. definitive vs. attingent presence as the question's unifying framework

HuYgTa-e82927-Dd1e211.summary: Article 1 (Utrum Deus sit in loco): establishes three conclusions on God's presence — God is not circumscriptively or determinatively in any place, because as simply infinite he cannot be commensurate with or restricted to place; God is in every place attingently and conservatively, since his infinite power reaches and sustains all things, as supported by Wisdom 8, the primacy of divine causality, and Augustine's and Anselm's accounts of divine containment; and being everywhere simply and per se is proper to God alone, a claim defended against objections from the soul's totality-in-body, the ubiquity of universals, the omnipresence of matter, and the temporal origin of created 'wheres,' each resolved by distinguishing per se/positive divine ubiquity from the merely per accidens, privative, or derivative presence of other things.
claims: God is neither circumscriptively nor determinatively located, being simply infinite.
God is present in every place by contact and conservation, in virtue of his infinite power.
Being everywhere per se and simply is a proprium belonging to God alone.

HuYgTa-e82927-Dd1e560.summary: Article 2 (Utrum angelus sit in loco): establishes three conclusions on angelic presence and motion. First, an angel is in place through the application of its power (a kind of relational, 'virtual' quantity) in operation, not through its bare essence — a position defended at length against ten counterarguments favoring an essence-based or operation-denying account, and against two rival opinions (universal non-local presence of order, and essence as immediate ground of location), with careful attention to reconciling the Parisian condemnations of 1277 with the author's (Aegidius Romanus's) view. Second, an angel's natural power confines it, like its species-determined nature, to one place at a time, a conclusion defended against objections drawn from the angel's mediate ontological status, from relational multiplicity, and from Eucharistic and glorified-body multilocation (all deflected as arguments from absolute rather than natural power, deferred to Book 4 d.10). Third, an angel is moved locally, a conclusion (matching Damascene and the analogy of the separated soul) whose proper temporal character is then debated at length: the author, following Aegidius Romanus, holds that angelic motion — both in its immanent acts of understanding/willing and its transient operations on bodies — occurs in time rather than in a bare instant, against a rival view arguing for instantaneous motion from the analogy of light, the incommensurability of angelic power and speed, and the soul's departure at death; each of the rival view's seven objections is judged individually inconclusive, though the temporal conclusion itself is retained, and Aegidius's own replies distinguish light's instantaneous-but-successive generation from angelic operation, deny the commensurability of angelic and corporeal time, and distinguish death as a mere mutatio from a genuine, temporally-measured motion.
claims: An angel is in place through the relational application of its power (virtual quantity) in operation, not through its bare substance.
An angel's natural power confines it to one place at a time.
An angel is moved locally, and this motion — both in the angel's immanent acts and its transient operations — occurs in time, not in an instant.
concepts: operation as ground of angelic location

HuYgTa-e82927-Dd1e2016.summary: Article 3 (Utrum anima rationalis sit in loco): a very brief and textually corrupt article stating that the conclusion regarding the rational soul's presence in place follows the same pattern already established for the angel in Article 2, without a separately developed proof.
claims: The rational soul is in place in the same manner (definitively, through operation) as the angel, by analogical extension of Article 2.
concepts: analogical extension from angelic to human-soul location

HuYgTa-e82927-Dd1e2040.summary: Article 4 (Utrum natura universalis sit in loco): concludes that universal nature is neither generated nor moved per se, but only derivatively insofar as the particulars in which it exists are generated and moved; closes the whole question by reconciling Boethius's claim that incorporeal things are not in place with the article-by-article conclusions, specifying that only circumscriptive location is thereby denied to spiritual substances.
claims: Universal nature is neither generated nor moved per se, but only through the generation/motion of the particulars instantiating it.

Boethius's denial that incorporeal things are in place should be read as denying only circumscriptive presence, consistent with the definitive and attingent-conservative presence established in the preceding articles.
concepts: reconciling authoritative texts across the question's four modes of presence

HuYgTa-e82927.summary: Quaestio 1, 'An substantia quaelibet spiritualis loco existat' (Whether any spiritual substance whatever exists in a place), resolves the question through four articles corresponding to the fourfold division of spiritual substance (uncreated/God, and created: intellectual/angel, rational/soul, universal nature). The overall resolutio, developed and defended across the articles, is that God is present everywhere attingently and conservatively but neither circumscriptively nor definitively, being alone the proper (per se, simple) possessor of ubiquity; an angel (and, by extension, the rational soul) is definitively — though never circumscriptively — located in place through the relational application of its power in operation rather than through bare essence, is confined by its natural power to one place at a time, and is moved locally, this motion occurring in time rather than in a bare instant; and universal nature, since it is neither generated nor moved per se, is likewise in place and in motion only derivatively, through the particulars that instantiate it. Boethius's dictum that incorporeal things are not in place is thus reconciled with the whole discussion by restricting its scope to circumscriptive location alone.
claims: Spiritual substance divides fourfold (God, angel, rational soul, universal nature), each requiring its own account of presence in place.
God alone possesses per se, simple ubiquity (attingent/conservative presence in every place, without circumscription or definition).

Angels and rational souls are definitively (not circumscriptively) located through the operative application of their power, are confined to one place at a time by natural power, and move locally in time.
Universal nature is in place and in motion only derivatively, through the particulars in which it exists.
